Advances in technology have led to the rise in a new era for genetically engineered crops in the U.S., which include incredible enhancements in herbicide-tolerant, insect-resistant, and nutritionally enhanced crops. While these innovations have greatly improved agricultural productivity, they raise a number of long-term health, environmental, and ethical considerations [@bawa2013genetically].

                                        By Maura Mann

![Source: https://brightgreenpartners.com/agricultural-biotechnology/](images/Afbeelding5-1.jpg){width=100%}

## Differing Research Priorities

We can look at the rise of genetically engineered crops through multiple angles and begin to understand how they took off in the first place. One of the reasons we have the technology to develop these types of crops is from the extensive resources dedicated towards making advancements in this field. While the total public sector agricultural and food research and development expenditure (adjusted for inflation) has decreased since the early 2000s, the private sector total food research and development expenditure (adjusted for inflation) has continued to rise.

![](plots/plot1.svg)

Decreases in public sector spending mean focuses such as food safety and regulations have taken a back seat to private sector focuses such as farm productivity, increasing crop protection, and optimizing food manufacturing processes. This has led to concerns over the lack of national body governing food systems and farmers being limited to growing private sector developed genetically engineered crops [@fuglie2016growing].

The question being investigated is whether increases in private food sector research & development expenditure have paved the way for increases in crop genetic engineering adoption. By exploring the time frame after the decline in public expenditure around 2000, we can isolate the trend through the percent of genetically engineered crops that were planted in the United States. While tackling this idea, we'll predominantly focus on a subset of crops, representing some of the most popular ones.

## Genetic Engineering: A Timeline

There are eleven genetically engineered crops that are available in the United States. They include corn, cotton, soybeans, canola, alfalfa, sugar beets, papaya, potatoes, apples, pineapples, and squash. When these crops are engineered, breeders identify genome variations of the crop that are most desirable. This informs the cross-breeding process where the ideal plants are created that can often avoid disease, insects, and prevent weed growth. Additionally, genetically engineering crops can make them last longer for the consumer such as some genetically engineered potatoes, which can be resistant to browning and bruising while they're being transported and even when cut in the kitchen [@U.S.Food&Drug].

![Source: Gemini Imagen 3 Model. Prompt: "Create a diagram for me that explains the steps of crop genetic engineering"](images/gemini.png){width=100%}

The diagram above outlines a genetic engineering process which includes: 1. DNA Extraction, 2. Gene Design, 3. Gene Transformation, 4. Cross-Breeding, and 5. Testing & Commercialization.

It wasn't always that genetically engineered crops made up the majority percentage of certain crops. Using corn as a case study, high corn producing states didn't start to plant mostly genetically engineered corn until around the early 2010s.

Move the slider below to see the percent of all corn planted that was genetically engineered from 2000 through 2025 by state.

However, ever since this trend towards planting genetically engineered corn started, there has not been a decrease. This trend also correlates with the increase in private food research and development expenditure. Interestingly, the further west states more quickly adopted genetically engineered corn although all states in general move in tandem.

In order to get a full picture, however, it's important to look at the trend of other crops in comparison throughout the wholr United States. As seen below when compared to corn, both cotton and soybeans had an even quick rise in the amount of genetically engineered crop that was being planted. Including cotton is helpful since it can be compared against two other food products in this case.

```{=html}
<iframe src="plots/plot3.html" width="85%" height="500px" frameborder="0" style="display:block; margin: 0 auto;"></iframe>
```

We can see from above that the rise in genetically engineered crops doesn't stop at food, even though that's what we initially observed the increase in private research expenditure for. Clearly, there is a larger trend in the agricultural space where plant genetic altering is being adopted on a larger scale by the entire farming industry.

It wouldn't be accurate to leave the analysis at just showing the increasing rise of planted genetically engineered crops. While what's shown above shows all genetically engineered varieties, we can narrow in on one type of genetically engineered trait and show how even within corn, cotton, and soybeans, industry trends change over time.

Click on one of the crop by state bars from 2025 to see its trend in U.S. farming from 2000.

```{=html}
<iframe src="plots/plot4.html" width="100%" height="800px" frameborder="0" style="display:block; margin: 0 auto;"></iframe>
```

While herbicide-tolerant engineered crops make up most of the current soybeans planted in the U.S., the same type of engineered crop has declined in recent years for corn and cotton. It turns out that there are cheaper ways to control weeds in corn and cotton fields due to way they're planted and how the fields can be maintained. The same cannot be said for soybeans and planting herbicide-tolerant crops has become the standard across the country [@USDA]. Therefore, the type of genetically engineered plants are highly dependent on profit margins regardless of the developments in technology. As much as the resources being dedicated towards this space have increased, if the technological advancements don't make sense financially, they won't be adopted on a large-scale by farmers.

## Financial Considerations

As seen above, there are financial considerations when it comes to planting genetically engineered crops. However, they have transformed the agriculture industry on both the manufacturing and consumer fronts. The U.S. farm income industry is huge, bringing in $1.53 trillon dollars in 2023, accounting for 5.3% of total GDP [@U.S.Chamber]. Some of the states with the largest farm-income are also some of the largest when it comes to planting genetically engineered corn, cotton, and soybeans.

![Green states are large GE corn, cotton, and soybean contributors. Orange are not large GE contributors.](plots/plot5.svg){width=100%}

The states that are large adopters are also more rural states and overall produce a lot of crops, but it's interesting to see that many of them keep up with each other when it comes to the trend in planting genetically engineered corn, cotton, and soybeans.

## Summary

Crop genetic engineering has transformed the agricultural and food industry from the early 2000s to now. While the crop footprint is small, more crops may become genetically enhanced as advancements are made. However, as many benefits are they bring, there remains public concern about their long-term harm.

## Conclusion

While genetically engineered crops are on the rise, they are only as beneficial as they make fiscal sense for farmers. In addition, the number of crops that are genetically engineered are still small and there are plenty of additional use cases for genetic engineering that haven't been fully explored such as climate-resistant crops. In a recent edition of the Trends in Plant Science academic journal, researchers stated that "..by the end of 2035, high-yielding, stress-resistant, and nutrient-efficient crops will be available for public use, helping to reduce hunger," indicating not only where genetic engineered crops can continue to improve in production quality, but how they can eventually be used to hopefully target larger hunger issues [@ahmar2026precision]. In this project, trends in genetic engineering adoption have primarily been explored up through 2025, but there is plenty of room for additional exploration in genetic engineering use cases and what future adoption looks like.
